geo_headlines: NO US STRIKES; MORE SHIPS HIT. No US strike on Iran was reported over the weekend. UKMTO counted at least 10 vessels attacked in or near Hormuz in the past week, the most since the war began in February, and a tug was hit by two projectiles off the UAE on Sunday (CBS). Iran reported tanker fires in Hormuz and the Sea of Oman on Saturday (Al Jazeera). **Brent ($109.86) and WTI ($101.41) reopen Sunday evening against that backdrop.**

TALKS: IRAN'S HORMUZ OFFER STILL ON THE TABLE. Foreign Minister Araghchi said Iran's proposal to reopen the strait within days is still on the table and that Tehran is reviewing US comments; Washington wants the nuclear program addressed first (Fox News). Trump left a Pickaxe Mountain strike on the table but ruled out ground troops (Al-Monitor).

SAUDI ARABIA UNDER FIRE. The Saudi-led coalition downed two drones overnight, one near Riyadh and one in the Eastern Province (Al Jazeera). The coalition says Riyadh's airport has been attacked 20 times this month (SBS). Rubio said Trump's 60-day Russia sanctions waiver reflects the strain on global oil prices (Al Jazeera).

AI FINANCING: ANTHROPIC AT 10%. Anthropic offered Blackstone a 10% coupon on $9 billion of junior debt in a $60 billion chip financing, up from 8.5% on a similar deal four months ago, the FT reported (via FourWeekMBA). That fits last week's theme: AI demand is strong, but the cost of financing it is rising.

FRIDAY RECAP: TECH'S WORST WEEK SINCE JUNE. S&P 500 7,659.44 (-1.09% Friday, -1.95% week), 2.04% below its October 6 record close; Nasdaq 100 -5.5% on the week; Dow +0.67%. VIX 19.99. 10-year 5.09%, down 15bp on the week. FedWatch, as of Friday: October hike 18.8%, December 84.8%. Bitcoin $81,974.

THIS WEEK: EARNINGS TEST THE AI STORY. Tuesday: GE Aerospace and GM before the open, Netflix after; November WTI expires. Wednesday: VIX options expire; Meta, Tesla, Texas Instruments, IBM after the close. Thursday: Procter & Gamble. Friday: American Express (StockTitan). Fed officials are in their pre-meeting quiet period ahead of October 27-28 (Federal Reserve).
client_frame_short: The weekend did not change the story. Tech had its worst week since June on worries about the cost of financing AI, while the Dow rose and bonds rallied. **The risk to watch when futures reopen Sunday evening is oil: ship attacks around Hormuz hit a wartime weekly high, Brent closed at $109.86, and there were no US strikes and no deal.** This week's earnings from Netflix, Meta and Tesla will test whether AI spending still pays. For clients, balanced portfolios held up as designed, and long-term plans do not need to change.
client_frame:
If a client calls today, the story is unchanged from Friday: a tech pullback inside a market that is otherwise holding together, with oil as the wild card.

Last week: the S&P 500 fell 1.95% and the Nasdaq 100 5.5%, the worst week for tech since June. The Dow rose 0.67%, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell from 5.24% to 5.09%, so bonds cushioned balanced portfolios. The S&P 500 is about 2% below its October 6 record close.

The AI question is about financing, not demand. Over the weekend the FT reported Anthropic offered a 10% coupon on $9 billion of junior debt, up from 8.5% four months ago. Money is still flowing to AI, but at a higher price, and that is what markets repriced last week.

Oil: at least 10 ships were attacked around Hormuz last week, the most since the war began, and Brent closed at $109.86. Iran says its offer to reopen the strait is on the table; Washington wants the nuclear program addressed first. Trump is talking about striking Pickaxe Mountain but has not. Higher fuel prices are feeding inflation, which is why markets price about an 85% chance of a December Fed hike.

This week: Netflix Tuesday, Meta and Tesla Wednesday, and VIX options expire Wednesday. With October options expired, markets may move more freely in both directions.

Why it matters: concentrated tech portfolios felt last week; diversified ones much less. Weeks like this are normal inside long bull markets, and selling into them has historically cost more than it saved.

For clients: stay invested, rebalance toward targets, and let high-quality bonds that pay about 5% do their job. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40% (Friday 5.09%), a 30-year above 5.75% (Friday 5.43%), or US strikes on Iran that keep Brent well above $105. Brent is already at $109.86; the missing piece is strikes.
